p.seg: Where there is something to yield, and something to hold firm,
then one can wield the power of the world.
Military affairs rely on power,
and power relies on geographical advantage.
Therefore, among the feudal lords, those who gain geographical advantage
will have power follow them;
those who lose geographical advantage
will have power leave them.
Those who contend for the world
must first contend for the people.
Those who understand the grand scheme will gain the people;
those who scrutinize petty calculations will lose the people.
Those who gain the support of the masses of the world become kings;
those who gain half of that support become hegemons.
Therefore, sagely kings humbly observe etiquette and employ the worthy of the world, entrusting them with responsibilities;
they distribute resources equitably to attract the masses of the world and make them their subjects.
Therefore, though they are honored as Sons of Heaven [tiān zǐ],
and possess the wealth of the world,
yet the world does not call them greedy,
for their grand scheme is preserved.
They use the wealth of the world
to benefit the people of the world;
they use the manifestation of manifest authority
to unite the power of the world;
they use the practice of developing virtue
To establish friendly relations with the various feudal lords;
To punish those guilty of treachery and flattery,
To set an example that would resonate in the hearts of all under Heaven;
To rely on the might of All under Heaven,
To extend the righteous campaigns of an enlightened king;
To attack rebellious and chaotic states,
To reward meritorious service;
To enshrine the virtue of the worthy and wise,
To illuminate the conduct of the one person (the ruler), and the common people will be settled.
Now, in the past, when the former kings took possession of All under Heaven,
How skillful and grand were their virtues!
It can be described as "material benefits".
Now, to ensure that a state is constantly free from calamity
and that both fame and profit arrive together,
This is divine sagacity (shén shèng).
If a state is in danger of collapse,
and yet it can endure,
This is enlightened sagacity (míng shèng).
Therefore, what the former kings emulated
was divine sagacity (shén shèng);
What they rewarded
was enlightened sagacity (míng shèng).
Now, a single word can prolong the life of a state,
Disregarding it leads to the state's demise;
Such a thing is the word of a great sage (dà shèng).
Now, what an enlightened ruler considers unimportant are horses and jade,
while what they consider important are governance and the military.
If a lost ruler is not like this,
they undervalue governing and entrust it to others,
while overvaluing horses and giving them to others;
they undervalue the military and entrust it to others,
while overvaluing jade and giving it to others;
they emphasize the construction of palace gates,
while undervaluing the defense of the four borders.
This is the reason for weakening.
Now, power is
what the divine and wise rely on.
Singular discernment is
the most effective tool in the world;
decisive action is
the stronghold for subtle and secret operations.
These two are what the sages emulate.
Sages are wary of the insignificant,
while fools fear the obvious;
the sages' hatred is inward,
while the fools' hatred is outward;
when a sage is about to act,
they are sure to know,
while a fool does not decline danger even when it is imminent.
Sages can assist the times,
but cannot go against the times.
The wise are good at planning,
but it is not as good as seizing the moment.
Those who make good use of time accomplish much with little time.
Now, if planning lacks direction, it will lead to difficulties;
if affairs are not prepared for, they will be abandoned.
Therefore, sagely kings strive to be fully prepared
and cautiously guard their timing.
Being prepared to await the opportune moment,
using the opportune moment to initiate affairs,
and launching troops when the time arrives;
destroying the strongholds and attacking the state,
defeating the large and controlling the territory;
establish large foundations, but aim small;
the land is close, yet attack the distant.
Use the large to control the small,
use the strong to command the weak,
use the many to overcome the few.
Virtue benefits the people,
power shakes the world;
orders are carried out among the feudal lords without resistance,
those nearby are all subdued,
those far away all obey.
Now, the wise king rectifies the world; this is the principle.
He supports the weak by relying on the strong,
To restrain violence and stop greed,
to ensure survival and resolve danger,
to continue interrupted lineages,
these are what the world esteems,
what the feudal lords participate in,
what the common people benefit from.
Therefore, the world crowns him king.
One whose knowledge covers the world,
whose judgment is the most decisive of his era,
whose talent resonates throughout the four seas,
is the assistant of a king.
If a state of a thousand chariots obtains his guardianship,
the feudal lords can be made his subjects,
and the world can be possessed.
If a state of ten thousand chariots loses his guardianship,
the state will no longer be its own.
If the world is all at peace
but one alone is in chaos,
that state will no longer be its own;
if the feudal lords are all united
but one alone is isolated,
that state will no longer be its own;
if neighboring states are all dangerous
but one alone is vulnerable,
The state is not what a state should be.
These three things
are signs of a state heading for ruin.
If the state is large
but its governance is small,
the state will follow its governance and become small.
If the state is small but its governance is large,
the state will become increasingly large.
Being large but not acting accordingly
will lead to shrinking again.
Being strong but not governing well
will lead to weakening again.
Having a large population but not governing well
will lead to dwindling numbers again.
Being noble but lacking propriety
will lead to becoming base again.
Having power but disregarding regulations
will lead to becoming insignificant again.
Being wealthy but arrogant and unrestrained
will lead to becoming poor again.
Therefore, to observe a state, observe its ruler;
to observe an army, observe its general;
to observe preparedness, observe the countryside.
If its ruler seems wise
but is not truly wise,
If their generals are like the worthy
but are not truly worthy,
if their people are like farmers
but are not truly farming,
if the three safeguards are already lost,
then the state is not their state.
If the land is vast but not cultivated,
it is called "earth full";
if the people are numerous but ungoverned,
it is called "people full";
if the military force is powerful but not righteous,
it is called "military full."
If the three fullnesses do not cease,
then the state is not their state.
If the land is vast but not cultivated,
it is not their land;
if the officials are noble but not subservient,
they are not their officials;
if the people are numerous but not close,
they are not their people.
Now, those who desire wealth without land should worry;
those who desire to be kings without virtue are in danger;
those who give sparingly but seek generously will be isolated.
Now, if superiors are oppressive and inferiors obstructive,
and if the state is small but the capital is large, then there will be regicide.
When the ruler is honored and the minister is humble,
when the superior is awe-inspiring and the subordinate is respectful,
so that commands are followed and people are obedient,
this is the ultimate in governance.
To have two emperors ruling the world,
the world cannot be governed;
to have two rulers in one state,
one state cannot be governed;
to have two fathers in one family,
one family cannot be governed.
Now, a command, if it is not lofty, will not be carried out;
if it is not forceful, it will not be heeded.
The people of Yáo 堯 and Shùn 舜
were not born able to govern;
the people of Jié 桀 and Zhòu 紂
were not born to create chaos.
Therefore, order or chaos lies with the superior.
Now, the foundation of hegemonic and kingly rule
takes the people as its basis.
If the basis is well-ordered, then the state is secure;
if the basis is chaotic, then the state is endangered.
Therefore, if the ruler is enlightened, then the subordinates are respectful;
if the government is just, then the people are at peace;
if the scholars are taught to be harmonious,
then the army will defeat the enemy;
If one employs the capable
, then all affairs are well-managed.
If one is close to the benevolent
, then the ruler will not be in danger.
If one appoints the worthy
, then the various lords will submit.
The model for a hegemon or a true king
is to surpass others through virtue and righteousness,
to surpass others through wisdom and strategy,
to surpass others through military prowess,
to surpass others through geographical advantages,
to surpass others through decisive actions.
Therefore, one becomes a true king.
Now, those who are good at managing a state
take advantage of the great state's importance,
to make it appear small in influence;
take advantage of the strong state's power,
to make it appear weak in influence;
take advantage of the heavy state's position,
to make it appear insignificant in influence.
If strong states are numerous
, one unites the strong to attack the weak
, in order to plan for hegemony.
If there are few strong states
Combining small forces to attack large ones
is a plan for becoming king.
If strong states are numerous
and one speaks of the might of kingship,
this is the wisdom of a fool.
If strong states are few
and one practices the way of a hegemon,
this is a plan for ruinous affairs.
Indeed, the divinely wise observe the shapes of the world
and know the timing of movement and stillness.
They observe the titles of precedence and subsequence
and know the gates of misfortune and fortune.
If strong states are numerous,
the one who moves first is in danger;
the one who moves later benefits.
If strong states are few,
the one who moves first becomes king;
the one who moves later perishes.
If warring states are numerous,
moving later can lead to hegemony.
If warring states are few,
moving first can lead to kingship.
Indeed, the heart of a king
is square and impartial, not prioritizing.
Rank does not yield to the worthy;
To consider worthy those who do not differentiate between younger brothers and to select from the masses
is to covet large possessions.
Therefore, the form of a king is great.
The former kings contended for the world
with rectitude,
they established it
with order,
and they governed it
with fairness and simplicity.
Establishing policies and issuing decrees
employed the way of humanity;
bestowing ranks and emoluments
employed the way of earth;
undertaking great affairs
employed the way of Heaven.
Therefore, the former kings in their military campaigns
attacked the rebellious, not the compliant;
attacked the dangerous, not the easy;
attacked the excessive, not the adequate.
Within the four borders,
they employed righteousness to manage them;
in assemblies of the feudal lords,
they employed authority to bring them about.
Those nearby who did not submit,
they troubled with (loss of) territory;
If those far away do not listen,
it is because their situation is perilous.
To attack them in two groups
and conquer them is
*wǔ* (martial);
to subdue
and then release them is
*wén* (civil);
when *wén* and *wǔ* are both fully realized,
that is *dé* (virtue).
The situation regarding the relative importance, strength, and weakness
is that when the lords unite, they are strong;
when isolated, they are weak.
Even with the talent of a *jì* (fine horse),
if a hundred horses take its place in rotation,
the *jì* will surely be exhausted;
if one is the strongest in an era,
but the whole world attacks it,
the state will surely be weakened.
A strong state gains by gathering the small,
but loses by relying on strength;
a small state gains by exercising restraint,
but loses by separating from the strong.
Now, whether a state is small or large, it must have plans;
whether strong or weak, it must have a strategy.
To subdue those near while strengthening those far is the characteristic of a hegemonic kingdom.
To unite the small to attack the large is the characteristic of adversarial states.
To use coastal states to attack coastal states is the characteristic of the central states (Zhōngguó).
To yield and serve the strong to avoid punishment is the characteristic of small states.
From ancient times until now, there has never been anyone
who could initiate difficulties first,
defy the times, change their form,
and thereby establish meritorious fame.
There has never been anyone who consistently
initiated difficulties first,
defied the times, changed their form,
and did not fail.
Now, desiring that a subject attack their ruler
and rectify the four seas,
one cannot conquer and seize by military force alone.
One must first determine strategy and planning,
be advantageous to the terrain,
make the weights of power beneficial,
be close to allied states,
To act according to the times
is the art of a true king.
Now, the campaigns of the former kings
were always launched with righteousness,
and carried out with swiftness.
Assessing the situation, they knew when it was permissible;
measuring their strength, they knew when to attack;
examining what they would gain, they knew the right time.
Therefore, the former kings' campaigns
always involved fighting a battle before attacking,
and attacking before seizing territory.
Thus, those skilled in attack
assess their troops to attack the enemy's troops,
assess their provisions to attack the enemy's provisions,
assess their defenses to attack the enemy's defenses.
When using troops to attack troops,
if the enemy's troops are strong, do not attack;
when using provisions to attack provisions,
if the enemy's provisions are plentiful, do not attack;
when using defenses to attack defenses,
if the enemy's defenses are secure, do not attack.
Abandon what is substantial and attack what is empty,
abandon what is strong and attack what is weak,
abandon what is difficult and attack what is easy.
To unite a nation does not depend on venerating the past,
Governing the world does not rely on being good at old practices;
becoming a hegemon or king does not rely on adhering to established norms.
Now, if actions are flawed, the state is endangered;
if punishments are excessive, authority is overturned;
if plans are changed easily, disaster will ensue;
if strategies succeed, faith in power is strengthened;
if accomplishments are achieved, fame will follow;
if authority is weighty, orders will be carried out;
this is the natural course of things.
Now, countries contending for strength
must first contend in strategy, contend in laws, and contend in authority.
To make the ruler happy or angry,
that is strategy (móu);
to make the state seem light or heavy,
that is law (xíng);
to make the army advance or retreat,
that is authority (quán).
Therefore, if one is skilled in strategy,
the ruler's desires can be attained,
and orders can be carried out;
if one is skilled in law,
the territory of a large state can be seized,
and the armies of a strong state can be resisted;
if one is skilled in authority,
the armies of the world can be aligned,
and the lords of the various states can be made to come to court.
Now, a sagely and wise ruler observes the state of the world,
understands the plots of the age,
knows where armies will attack,
knows where lands will be annexed,
and knows where decrees will be enforced.
An army that attacks what it hates
for its own benefit
will not be befriended by neighboring states.
A power that acts on what it dislikes
and finds few submitting to it is merely strong.
One who single-handedly destroys a state
and whose strength endures in later generations is a king.
One who single-handedly destroys a state
and whose strength benefits neighboring states will perish.
Question 24, seven statements on internal affairs.
In establishing a court,
inquire into the fundamental principles.
If titles are bestowed on those with virtue,
then great ministers will be motivated by righteousness;
if emoluments are given to those with merit,
then scholars will readily die for their principles;
if the ruler leads his scholars with what people esteem,
then superiors and inferiors will be in harmony;
if responsibilities are assigned according to ability,
then people will strive for achievement.
If punishment is carefully matched to the crime,
then people will not readily engage in litigation;
if the altars of the state and ancestral temples are not disrupted,
then people will have something to revere.
If one does not attend to the seasons (tiānshí),
then wealth will not be produced.
If one does not attend to the advantages of the land (dìlì),
then the granaries will not be full.
If the fields are uncultivated and desolate,
then the people will be uncivilized.
If the ruler has no limits,
then the people will be reckless.
If clever rhetoric is not restrained,
then the people will become licentious.
If the two sources (liǎngyuán) are not blocked,
then punishments will become numerous.
If one does not understand ghosts and spirits (guǐshén),
then the ignorant people will not be enlightened.
If one does not revere the mountains and rivers (shānchuān),
then authority and commands will not be heard.
If one does not respect the ancestral temples (zōngmiào),
then the people will challenge their superiors.
If one is not respectful to the ancestors and elders (zǔjiù),
then filial piety and fraternal duty will not be complete.
If the four cardinal principles are not upheld,
the state will perish.
End of "Ode to the State".
The state has four cardinal principles.
If one of the cords is cut, there is tilting;
if two are cut, there is danger;
if three are cut, there is overturning;
if four are cut, there is destruction.
Tilting can be corrected,
danger can be made secure,
overturning can be righted,
but destruction cannot be restored.
What are the Four Cardinal Virtues?
The first is Lǐ (禮, propriety),
the second is Yì (義, righteousness),
the third is Lián (廉, integrity),
the fourth is Chǐ (恥, shame).
Lǐ (禮) does not exceed measure,
Yì (義) does not advance oneself,
Lián (廉) does not conceal evil,
Chǐ (恥) does not follow what is crooked.
Therefore, if one does not exceed measure
then the ruler is secure;
if one does not advance oneself
then the people have no cunning deceit;
if one does not conceal evil
then conduct is naturally complete;
if one does not follow what is crooked
then evil affairs do not arise.
The above is the Four Cardinal Virtues.
The success of governance
lies in aligning with the people's desires;
the failure of governance
lies in going against the people's desires.
The people detest worry and toil,
I provide them with ease and joy;
the people detest poverty and lowliness,
I enrich and ennoble them;
the people detest danger and collapse,
I preserve and secure them;
the people detest extinction,
I help them thrive and multiply.
If one can provide them with ease and joy,
then the people will take on worry and toil for them;
if one can enrich and ennoble them,
then the people will endure poverty and lowliness for them;
if one can preserve and secure them,
then the people will face danger and collapse for them;
if one can help them thrive and multiply,
then the people will risk extinction for them.
Therefore, punishments are insufficient to instill fear in their intentions,
executions are insufficient to subdue their hearts.
Thus, if punishments are numerous yet intentions are not fearful,
then orders will not be carried out;
If you slaughter the masses and their hearts are not won over,
then the position of the ruler is in danger.
Therefore, comply with their four desires,
then those far away will naturally become close;
engage in their four aversions,
then those nearby will betray you.
Therefore, knowing that giving is the way to take,
is the treasure of governance.
The above are the Four Compliances.
To establish the state on an unshakeable foundation,
to accumulate in inexhaustible granaries,
to store in unfailing treasuries,
to issue commands at the source of flowing water,
to employ the people in offices free from contention,
to clarify the path of certain death,
to open the gate of certain gain,
do not strive for what cannot be achieved,
do not seek what cannot be obtained,
do not dwell where one cannot last,
do not proceed where one cannot return.
To establish the state on an unshakeable foundation
is to entrust those with virtue.
To accumulate in inexhaustible granaries
is to diligently cultivate the five grains.
To store in unfailing treasuries
To cultivate mulberry and hemp, and to raise the six domestic animals.
To issue orders at the source of the flowing water
is to ensure that the orders comply with the hearts of the people.
To employ the people in positions where there is no contention
is to enable each to develop their strengths.
To clearly define the path that leads to certain death
is to enforce strict punishments.
To open the gate to certain attainment
is to make rewards trustworthy.
Not to attempt what cannot be achieved
is to assess the people's strength.
Not to seek what cannot be obtained
is not to force the people to do what they hate.
Not to dwell in what cannot last long
is not to steal for a single generation.
Not to do what cannot be undone
is not to deceive the people.
Therefore, if you entrust power to the virtuous
the state will be secure.
If you dedicate efforts to the five grains
food will be sufficient.
If you cultivate mulberry and hemp,
and raise the six domestic animals,
the people will be prosperous.
If the orders comply with the hearts of the people,
Then authority and commands are carried out.
If you cause the people to each do what they are good at,
then resources are complete.
If punishments are strict,
then the people will stay away from evil.
If rewards are trustworthy,
then the people will take difficulties lightly.
If you assess the people's strength,
then there is nothing that cannot be accomplished.
If you do not force the people to do what they dislike,
then fraud and deceit will not arise.
If you do not steal for a single generation,
then the people will have no resentment in their hearts.
If you do not deceive the people,
then those below will be close to those above.
The above are eleven principles.
To manage a family as one would a village, then the village cannot be managed.
A xiāng (鄉 village) cannot be managed if you manage it like a family.
To manage a village (xiāng) as one would a state (guó), then the state cannot be managed.
A guó (國 state) cannot be managed if you manage it like a xiāng (鄉 village).
To manage a state (guó) as one would the world (tiānxià), then the world cannot be managed.
Tiānxià (天下 the world) cannot be managed if you manage it like a guó (國 state).
Manage a family as a family should be managed,
manage a village (xiāng) as a village (xiāng) should be managed,
Govern the state as (you would) govern a state,
govern all under Heaven as (you would) govern all under Heaven.
Do not say (people are) not of the same kind,
(for) those far away will not listen;
do not say (people are) not from the same village,
(for) those far away will not act;
do not say (people are) not from the same state,
(for) those far away will not follow.
Be like the earth, be like the sky,
how (can there be) selfishness or favoritism?
Be like the moon, be like the sun,
(adhere to) only the principles of the ruler.
The reins for controlling the people
lie in what the ruler values;
the doorway for guiding the people
lies in what the ruler prioritizes;
the road for summoning the people
lies in what the ruler likes and dislikes.
Therefore, if the ruler seeks it,
then the ministers will obtain it;
if the ruler craves it,
then the ministers will consume it;
if the ruler likes it,
then the ministers will wear it;
If the ruler hates something,
then his ministers will hide it from him.
Do not conceal your faults,
do not change your standards,
then worthy men will not assist you.
If words fill a room,
if words fill a hall,
this is called a sagely king.
City walls and moats
are insufficient for secure defense,
armor and strong forces
are insufficient to meet the enemy,
vast territory and much wealth
are insufficient to possess the people;
only one who possesses the Dao
can prepare for calamity before it takes shape,
therefore disaster does not sprout.
The world is not worried about a lack of ministers,
but worries about a lack of a ruler to employ them;
the world is not worried about a lack of wealth,
but worries about a lack of people to distribute it.
Therefore, one who understands the times
can be established as a leader;
one who is impartial
can be placed in charge of governance;
To be discerning of the times and observant of their usefulness,
and able to fill official positions,
is one who can be revered as a ruler.
The slow are behind in affairs;
those stingy with wealth lose their relatives;
those who trust petty people lose worthy men.
The above is about the six relations and five principles.
The second classic on Form and Situation
says two things.
XSJ
Mountains
are the tallest of things.
Kindness
is the ruler's loftiest conduct.
Benevolence is the parents' loftiest conduct.
Loyalty is the subordinates' loftiest conduct.
Filial piety
is the children's loftiest conduct.
Therefore, if the mountain is high and does not collapse,
then prayers are answered.
If the ruler is kind and does not waver,
then the people obey.
If parents are benevolent and do not waver,
then the children are obedient.
If subordinates are loyal and do not waver,
then rank and emolument arrive.
If a daughter-in-law is filial but unyielding
, then a good name is attached [to her];
therefore, if integrity is lofty but unyielding
, then what is desired will be obtained.
If (one) yields, then (one) will not obtain (it).
Therefore, it is said: If a mountain is high and does not collapse,
then sacrificial sheep will arrive;
if an abyss is deep and does not dry up,
then submerged jade will reach its limit (i.e., be abundant).
XSJ
An abyss
is where many things are born;
if it can be deep and not dry up,
then submerged jade will arrive.
A ruler
is the one on whom people rely to live.
If (the ruler) can be generous, magnanimous, sincere, and honest, and not harsh or jealous,
then the people will attach themselves (to the ruler).
Parents
are those from whom sons and daughters-in-law receive instruction;
if (parents) can be loving, benevolent, and instruct without losing principle,
then the sons and daughters-in-law will be filial.
Ministers and subordinates
are those whom the ruler employs;
if (they) can exert their utmost effort in serving their superiors,
Then they are fitting to the lord.
A daughter-in-law,
is the means by which parents are comforted.
If she is able to be filial, fraternal, and obedient to her parents-in-law,
then she is fitting to them.
Therefore, if a pool dries up and has no water,
then submerged jade will not arrive.
If a lord is harsh and without generosity,
then the myriad people will not submit.
If parents are violent and without kindness,
then the daughter-in-law will not be close.
If subordinates follow along without loyalty,
then they will be humiliated, disgraced, and impoverished.
If a daughter-in-law does not bring comfort to her parents-in-law,
then misfortune and worry will arrive.
Therefore, if a pool does not dry up,
then what is desired will arrive.
If it dries up,
then it will not arrive.
Therefore, it is said:
"If a pool is deep and does not dry up,
then submerged jade will reach its limit."
If Heaven does not change its constancy,
XSJ
Heaven covers all things,
regulates cold and heat,
moves the sun and moon,
arranges the stars,
this is the constancy of Heaven;
governing it with principle,
it ends and begins again.
The ruler governs the myriad people,
governs the world,
oversees the hundred officials,
this is the constancy of the ruler;
governing it with law,
it ends and begins again.
Harmonizing descendants,
connecting relatives,
this is the constancy of parents;
governing it with righteousness,
it ends and begins again.
Being earnest, respectful, loyal, and trustworthy,
this is the constancy of ministers and subordinates.
Serving their ruler with this,
it ends and begins again.
Loving parents, treating them well and providing for them,
thinking respectfully and following their teachings,
this is the constancy of children and wives;
To serve one's parents,
from beginning to end and again from the beginning.
Therefore, if Heaven does not lose its constancy,
then cold and heat obtain their proper times,
and the sun, moon, and stars obtain their proper order.
If the ruler does not lose his constancy,
then the assembled ministers obtain their righteousness,
and the hundred officials guard their duties.
If parents do not lose their constancy,
then sons and grandsons are harmonious and obedient,
and relatives rejoice with each other.
If ministers and subordinates do not lose their constancy,
then affairs are without fault,
and official duties are well-governed.
If sons and daughters-in-law do not lose their constancy,
then elders and juniors are ordered and close relatives and distant relatives are harmonious.
Therefore, those who employ constancy govern,
and those who lose constancy are in chaos.
Heaven has never changed that by which it governs,
therefore it is said:
Heaven does not change its constancy.
XS
Earth does not alter its rules;
XSJ
Earth gives birth to and nourishes the myriad things;
The rule of Earth.
To govern and pacify the people
is the rule of the ruler.
To teach and protect family affairs
is the rule of the parents.
To remonstrate uprightly and die for principle
is the rule of the ministers.
To exert oneself and provide sustenance
is the rule of the sons and daughters-in-law.
If the Earth does not change its rule,
